then.text: Width of the pool by Christmas, that's the plan. Don't tell the ducks. They'd only gloat.

else.text: Keeper Maud is on a bench by the duck pond in a towelling robe, a swimming cap pulled down over her ears. She looks shifty.
{player}! Don't look at the cap. Sit down. Can you keep a secret? I've held the Brook Stone for forty years, and I can't swim.
Never could. I stand in the shallow end looking wise. Nobody's noticed. So I've started lessons. Tuesdays, with the toddlers. I'm top of the class.
One of them bit me, but we've sorted it out. My lot have been practising too, to keep me company. Give them a proper splash, would you?
Lovely. Here, a bottle of my cordial, and how to make it. Elderflower and spring water. It won't help you swim, but it helps with most else.

then.text: Saturday, Cavern-ish, eight o'clock. Me mam's bringing the ferret. The ferret's got a better seat than me.

else.text: Keeper Ray is sitting by the bronze Beatles with a notebook, chewing a pencil down to splinters.
Alright, la. Don't laugh. I'm writing a song. Me mam's eighty on Saturday and she says one more drum solo and she's moving to Birkenhead.
First line's done: 'Mam, you raised five lads and a ferret.' I'm stuck on the next. Go on, you're good with words. Well, you're good with something.
Finish Ray's line?

then.text: 'And we never deserved it.' Oh, that's... hang on. Something in me eye. It's the Mersey. It gets everywhere.
The sherry! She'll go mad. She'll love it. That's the chorus, that is. Everyone can join in, they all know about the sherry.

else.text: 'Have a biscuit.' Doesn't rhyme, doesn't scan. She'll love it. She loves a biscuit more than any of us.
Here, have some of me mam's scouse, and the recipe. She says if I'm giving it away, give it to someone who'll do it right.

then.text: I booked the little train. Window seat, the side away from the drop. That's what you call planning.

else.text: Keeper Eluned is on a bench by the quarry, staring up at Yr Wyddfa as if it owes her money.
Shwmae. Sit if you want. Forty years in that quarry and I've never been up the mountain. Not once. Don't tell anyone. Especially the mountain.
Heights. Down a pit, I'm fine. Put me on a ladder and I go like a jelly in a tumble dryer. You've been to the top. What's it like?
What's it like at the summit?

then.text: A cafe. Well. That changes things. I'll not go up for the view, but I'll go up for a Welsh cake.
Four countries. Ireland, England, the Isle of Man, and us in the middle looking smug. Right. The little train, then. Eyes shut.

else.text: Every step. You would say that, you've the legs of a goat. Go on, then. I'll go up. Slowly. Swearing in two languages.
Here. My taid's lamp from the quarry. He said it saw him home every night for fifty years. It'll do more good with you than in my shed.

then.text: We lost the match fourteen nil. Nobody cried. Well. I did, a bit. Proud, see.

else.text: Keeper Rhys is in Bute Park with a bag of cones, a whistle, and an ice pack strapped to one knee.
Ah, {player}! Don't mind the knee. Doctor says I've the knees of a man twice my age. I said, which man? He said, a retired one.
So I'm coaching the under-nines now. Twelve kids, one ball, no tactics whatsoever. Best thing I've done in years.
I promised them a demonstration before their big match. Fancy being the opposition? Go easy. Actually, don't. They'll know.
Lovely stuff. They'll be talking about that for weeks. Mostly about my knee. Here, the team insisted. Wear it on match days.

then.text: Chapter nine. The Warden takes off his lanyard. Slowly. I'll say no more.

else.text: Keeper Morwen is on a bench near the Chalice Well, typing furiously on an old laptop. She snaps it shut as you arrive.
You saw nothing. Fine, you saw something. I write novels, love. Romance. Thirty-one of them. Heaving bosoms and brooding farmers, mostly.
{rival} bought one at the station, read it on the train and had to get off at Taunton for a lie-down. Go on, guess my pen name.
Morwen's pen name?

then.text: Close. Rosamund Thornbury. Thorne was taken by a woman in Frome who writes about vets. We don't speak.
Ha! Too much. Even I have limits. It's Rosamund Thornbury. Lady Avalon is my sister, and she's far worse.

else.text: Dave. I nearly did, you know. Nobody suspects a Dave. It's Rosamund Thornbury, but I'll think of you at the next contract.
Here. I pressed this clover in my first manuscript for luck. It's done its job. Book thirty-two is about a Warden who learns to love. Don't laugh.

then.text: She laughed at three of my jokes. Three! We're going to the pictures Thursday. I'm not a doctor, but I think that's serious.

else.text: Keeper Declan is on a bench in St Stephen's Green in his good jacket, flattening his hair with one hand. He looks like a man about to sit an exam.
Ah, it's yourself. Thank God. I've a date. A real one, with Brid from the hurling club. First in thirty years. My hands are like two wet haddock.
My sister says bring flowers. My nephew says bring nothing, it's 'too much'. What would you do?
What should Declan do?

then.text: Flowers. Grand. Sensible. Daffodils. Nobody ever got in trouble over a daffodil.
A bowl of stew. On a date. ...Do you know, she did say she likes a man who can cook. You're either a genius or a lunatic.

else.text: Myself. God help her. Right. Right so. Myself, but in the good jacket.
Here, take this pin. My mother gave it me for luck the day I got the Kin Stone. Go on, before I lose my nerve and give you the jacket too.

then.text: Out on the bay tomorrow, if it's calm. If it's not, sure, she'd have gone anyway.

else.text: Keeper Nuala is by the docks with an old currach upside down on two trestles, a pot of tar, and a face like a storm warning.
Dia dhuit. Grab the other end, would you? She was my grandmother's boat. The very one she rowed to Inis Mor in the gale. She's leaking like a gossip.
Help with the currach?
options: Hold it steady and hum a shanty

then.text: You hum. Nuala joins in on the second verse, badly, and the gulls leave in protest.

else.text: There. Tight as a drum. Granny would've said I tarred it like a Dub. That was the worst thing she ever called anyone.
I take her out once a year, on Granny's day. Just to the mouth of the bay and back. I say hello to the water and tell her who won the hurling.
Take this. Granny wove it, and it hung over our door forty years. She'd want it out on the road, not on a nail. She hated sitting still.

then.text: She's called the Wee Samson. Forty-one hours, that one. The tweezers have earned a pension.

else.text: Keeper Ruairí is on a bench by the slipways, squinting through a magnifying glass at a tiny ship in a bottle. His enormous hands are very, very still.
Bout ye. Whisht a second. ...There. Mainsail's up. Forty years building the big ones, and at night I build them small. Don't tell the apprentices.
It's the patience I like. You can't rush a ship in a bottle, and you can't rush iron. My lot think I've gone soft, mind.
They've been up all night watching me with the tweezers, and they're raging. Give them a run out, would you? Let them blow off steam.
That's them settled. Here, a horseshoe off the yard gate. Points up, so the luck doesn't run out. You've plenty, but it never hurts.

then.text: The scarf's for Gordon's new wife. It's eleven feet long. That's not a message. It's just a very long scarf.

else.text: Keeper Isla is on a bench on the Ness Islands, knitting something long and tartan at an alarming speed.
Oh, it's you. Sit, sit. I told you those waders outlived two husbands. Folk have been sending me sympathy cards.
They're not dead! Gordon's in Elgin with a woman who does pottery, and Alasdair runs a chippy in Nairn. Lovely men. Couldn't sweep to save their lives.
Gordon's getting married again next month, and I'm going to win the dancing. My team needs a warm-up first. So do I. Sweep hard!
That'll do. Here, a thistle brooch. Wear it to a wedding and nobody dares sit you next to the ex.

then.text: The walk's at seven. I've added a stop for the Champion of the Moot. I tell them you're friendly. You are, mostly.

else.text: Keeper Hester is on a bench by the Minster, her top hat on her knee, watching the pigeons with the tired look of someone up since the Romans.
Hello, love. Champion of the Moot, and you still come and sit with an old woman. Can I tell you something I've never told the walk?
Thirty years leading the ghost walk, and I've never seen one. Not one. I hear them. I talk to them. But I've never seen so much as a sheet.
Some nights I wonder if I'm only a woman in a hat telling stories in the cold. Sit a minute. Listen with me. What do you hear?
What do you hear?

then.text: Humming. Yes. That'll be the Roman lad by the wall. Tone deaf, bless him. Thank you, love. That's the nicest thing anyone's done for me since 1994.

else.text: Nothing. Well, that's honest. And do you know, I think that's them being polite. They don't like to interrupt. Thank you for listening, all the same.
Take this hag stone. Look through the hole and you see the spirits, they say. I've looked for thirty years. Tell me if you have better luck.

then.text: Four hundred and thirteen. I found one in my own pocket. Old stock. I've logged it.

else.text: Gareth Pryce is on a bench by the mountain railway in a hi-vis vest, a litter picker in one hand and a clipboard in the other. Old habits.
Ah. You. I suppose you'll want an explanation. I'm volunteering. The glass offices are a soft play now, and I have feelings. I've put them in a spreadsheet.
Crisp packets collected on Yr Wyddfa this month: four hundred and twelve. Last year I was dropping them, so that's infinite improvement. Will you sign my timesheet?
Sign Pryce's timesheet?
options: Sign it with a smiley face

then.text: Signed. By an actual Champion. I shall frame it next to my old lanyard, which I keep in a drawer as a warning.

else.text: A smiley face. On a timesheet. That's irregular. I'll allow it. Don't tell anyone, I've a reputation for misery to keep up.
Here. The volunteer coordinator gave me this acorn and said I needed to grow as a person. Rude, but accurate. You have it.

then.text: The knockers ate the pasty and left the note. I've decided that means I'm forgiven. The crab disagrees.

else.text: Sir Rupert Ashcombe is on a bench by the harbour, hat off, crabbing line in the water, a child's bucket at his feet. The crab in it looks in charge.
Don't. I know how it looks. I've been asked to 'take some time to reflect'. By my wife. And the board. And, in a dream, by a very small miner with a lamp.
I've given Geevor back every ounce of tin, and I'm leaving the knockers a pasty and a note. Help me sign it off, would you?
How should Ashcombe sign it?
options: Sorry about the drill, love, Rupert

then.text: Sincerely. Yes. Stiff, but sincere. Like the hat.
Apologetically. Quite right. I've never written that word before. It has a lot of letters for something so small.

else.text: 'Sorry about the drill, love, Rupert.' Oh, that's dreadful. They'll adore it. I'll put in an extra pasty.
Here. I found this pearl in a sealskin pouch on the beach this morning. They say its owner may come back for it. I've had enough of keeping things that aren't mine.

then.text: He's eaten another rose. The castle has sent a letter. I'm going to reply to it. Slowly. In full sentences.

else.text: Siobhán Kerrigan is on a bench in the rose garden in wellies, holding a lead rope. On the end of it is a donkey, eating a rose with enormous dignity.
Ah. {player}. Yes, it's a donkey. I handed in my lanyard and walked straight into a donkey sanctuary. They asked if I could do spreadsheets. I said, I'm afraid so.
This one came in last week. Thirty years old, one ear up, and no name. I've been calling him Item Four. Will you name him?
Name the donkey?

then.text: Bartholomew. He likes it, look. The ear went up. Both ears, nearly.
Lanyard. Oh, that's cruel. That's perfect. I'll put it on the board under all the saints and see who notices.

else.text: Kevin. Like St Kevin of Glendalough, who let a blackbird nest in his hand. Yes. Kevin.
I bake for the open days now. My granny's barmbrack. Have some, and the recipe. If you find the ring, you are not marrying the donkey.

then.text: Forty-two rescues this year. One was the same man from Surrey, twice. He's bought boots now. Progress.

else.text: Morag Strachan is on a bench on the High Street in her waxed jacket, a mountain rescue badge sewn on the arm, muttering at a notebook.
Don't look so surprised. Mountain rescue. Tuesdays, and whenever a man from Surrey goes up Ben Nevis in flip-flops. Which is most days.
And I'm learning Gaelic. Years drawing lines on maps of places I couldn't even say. Hear me out: Tha mi duilich. It means 'I'm sorry'.
How was that?
options: Say it like you mean it

then.text: Spot on. Liar. Kind liar. I'll take it. I've a lot of people to say it to, and the hills are top of the list.

else.text: Like I mean it. Aye. That was always the hard bit. Tha mi duilich. ...There. That one I meant.
Have this rowan sprig. The old folk tied it over the byre to keep harm off. I spent years being the harm. Now I'm handing them out.

then.text: I've packed. Unpacked. Packed again. The suitcase has been as far as the front step. Small steps, {player}.

else.text: Professor Garside is on a bench in the middle of Macclesfield with a flask, a packet of custard creams and, for once, nowhere to be.
{player}. Sit. Have a biscuit. This is the first Tuesday in twenty years I haven't had to keep the old places safe. I don't know what to do with my hands.
Twenty years as Champion and never one holiday. Every time I packed a bag, something woke up and growled. So. A whole fortnight. Where should I go?
Where should Garside go?

then.text: Hot, with a pool. I'll burn like a crumpet in four minutes, but I'll be a happy crumpet.
A caravan in Wales. Rain on the roof, a kettle, and Eluned an hour away to tell me off. Perfect.

else.text: Feet up in my own kitchen, with nobody ringing the wireless. Do you know, that might be the most daring thing of all.
Here. I nailed this horseshoe over the Champion's seat at the Moot twenty years ago, points up so the luck couldn't run out. It didn't. It's yours now. So's the seat.
